section_summaries.epidemiology: Human African trypanosomiasis (HAT) is an important neglected tropical disease caused by protozoal parasites of the genus Trypanosoma and transmitted by tsetse flies (Glossina spp.). The two human pathogens are T. b. gambiense (causing chronic infection) and T. b. rhodesiense (causing acute disease), while T. b. brucei is primarily an animal pathogen. Trypanosomes are flagellated, extracellular protozoa that multiply in the bloodstream and undergo morphological and antigenic changes in the tsetse fly vector. Tsetse flies are found in microfoci between 14°N and 29°S, with G. morsitans, G. fuscipes, and G. palpalis being important vectors. Their behavior and ecology, including preference for warm temperatures, shade, and humidity, influence the epidemiology. A small proportion of flies are competent to transmit the infection.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Normal human plasma contains a trypanolytic factor, made of apolipoprotein L1, apolipoprotein A-I, and haptoglobin-related protein, which lyses animal trypanosomes. Pathogenic T. brucei subspecies have developed genetic resistance to this human trypanolytic factor. Parasites also evade the host immune system through a dense surface coat of glycoprotein (variant surface glycoprotein or VSG), which undergoes antigenic variation via programmed DNA rearrangements. This constant antigenic switching leads to chronic stimulation of the host's immune system, hypergammaglobulinemia, and exhaustion of defense mechanisms. Trypanosomes penetrate privileged sites like the central nervous system, and IgM and IgG antibodies are directed to non-VSG antigens, leading to rheumatoid factor-like reactivity, anti-DNA antibodies, and heterophile antibodies, which can cause misleading serologic test results.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: HAT presents with a wide range of differential diagnoses, often with an insidious onset, and is invariably fatal if untreated. Clinical staging is crucial. A local reaction, the trypanosomal chancre, can develop at the tsetse bite site, appearing as a raised papule with erythema, local edema, and regional lymphadenopathy. Chancres are more common in T. b. rhodesiense and heal without treatment in weeks. The hemolymphatic stage (HAT Stage I) of T. b. rhodesiense can manifest dramatically with fever and symptoms resembling falciparum malaria or septicemia, potentially leading to death from cardiac involvement within weeks. T. b. gambiense infection is usually milder initially. Symptoms include undulating fever, lymph node enlargement (Winterbottom's sign), patchy rash, myxedematous infiltration ('puffy face syndrome'), and delayed hyperesthesia (Kérandel's sign). The meningoencephalitic stage (HAT Stage II) involves cerebral involvement, occurring within weeks for T. b. rhodesiense and months to years for T. b. gambiense. Symptoms include increasing headache, behavioral/personality changes, and neurological deficits (focal or generalized). MRI shows hyperintense signals in white matter, internal capsule, basal ganglia, and cerebellum. Histologically, perivascular infiltration ('cuffing') and glial proliferation occur. Late-stage symptoms include confusion, agitation, inability to perform simple tasks, circadian rhythm dysfunction, sleep fragmentation, somnolence, coma, progressive wasting, and dehydration. Morular cells of Mott can be found in CSF.
section_summaries.diagnosis: A confirmed diagnosis of African trypanosomiasis is critical due to complicated patient management and toxic treatments. Clinical suspicion arises in patients from or returning from endemic areas. The first step distinguishes between T. b. rhodesiense (acute, chancre, high fever, easily detectable parasites) and T. b. gambiense (chronic, non-specific symptoms, scanty parasitemia). Parasites can be sought in chancre aspirate, lymph node aspirates (e.g., posterior cervical nodes forming Winterbottom's sign), blood films (thick films for T. b. rhodesiense; concentration techniques for T. b. gambiense), and CSF. Concentration methods include mini anion exchange columns, quantitative buffy coat (QBC), and capillary tube centrifugation (CTC), often combined with fluorescence labeling. Nucleic acid amplification techniques like PCR and LAMP are being investigated for low parasite abundance. Serologic assays, such as the card agglutination test for trypanosomiasis (CATT), are reliable for T. b. gambiense screening but not for T. b. rhodesiense. Novel rapid diagnostic tests (HAT Sero-K-SeT, SD Bioline HAT 1.0) are >90% sensitive and useful for passive screening.
section_summaries.treatment: Treatment for HAT is challenging and hazardous, often requiring hospitalization due to drug side effects and the patient's critical condition. Early diagnosis improves cure rates. Stage I HAT caused by T. b. gambiense is treated with Pentamidine, given by intramuscular or intravenous infusion, achieving high cure rates (98%). T. b. rhodesiense Stage I is treated with Suramin, administered intravenously. Both Pentamidine and Suramin do not reach therapeutic levels in CSF. Stage II HAT, for both T. b. gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense, has historically been treated with Melarsoprol, an arsenical compound, despite its high rate of serious adverse effects (5–14% acute encephalopathy), and increasing resistance. Glucocorticosteroids (prednisolone) can reduce mortality. Eflornithine (DFMO) is an anti-tumor agent used for melarsoprol-refractory T. b. gambiense cases, not effective for T. b. rhodesiense due to higher ornithine decarboxylase turnover. Nifurtimox is a second-line treatment or partner in combination therapies for T. b. gambiense. NECT (nifurtimox-eflornithine combination therapy) is now the preferred first-line treatment for stage II T. b. gambiense HAT. New oral treatments like Fexinidazole and investigational oxaborole are being developed to reduce adverse effects and improve applicability.
section_summaries.prevention: Chemoprophylaxis with pentamidine or suramin is no longer recommended. Individual protection involves using insect repellents, wearing long-sleeved, bright clothing, and avoiding known infested land. Although HAT among tourists is rare, it is reported in returned travelers from game parks. Control efforts in endemic areas involve public health measures, mass screening, vector control (trapping, insecticide spraying), and active case finding by mobile teams. This strategy aims to deplete the parasite reservoir and interrupt transmission. Despite past successes in interrupting transmission, resurgences due to war and civil unrest, combined with decreasing drug availability, pose a continued threat.

rows: Zoonosis; wild (antelopes, e.g., bushbuck) and occasionally domestic animals as reservoir and source of case clusters; epidemic outbreaks, mainly in East Africa (Tanzania, Zambia, Malawi). Infrequent risk for safari/game park visitors.
Mainly anthroponosis with evidence for several other mammal species (e.g., pigs); severe public health problem in some West and Central African countries (DRC, Sudan, Angola, CAR, Chad).
Transmitted by savannah tsetse flies (Morsitans group).

Acute onset, fever, chancre frequent, rapid progression; death frequently in stage I (cardiac failure) in the first weeks.
Febrile disease, slow progression; death usually in stage II after many months or years.
Parasites usually in high number and easily detectable, serologic tests unreliable.
Parasitemia scanty, serology reliable in later stages.
